compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
This table covers six observation points inside the meeting, with the conditions fixed: the same people, the same matter, the same two available windows, A and B. If one of them is convening and the other merely invited, or one has been on this team for three years, role and experience will swamp both columns. The rows describe evidence that may get more attention, not who speaks earlier or executes better; either type may take either approach in the same row.

| Observation point in the meeting | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ISTP: evidence likely to be attended to first | Which axis this row lands on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to hold this call, and for how long | Weigh how each workable meeting option affects those who would otherwise be left out | Apply the same criteria for synchronous discussion to all workable options | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both plan the same meeting while the same papers are pending | Agree on a provisional agenda and a time to revisit it | Keep two workable agenda options open until the papers arrive | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both review the same mismatch in the report | Look for a pattern across comparable discrepancies and list possible shared causes | Check the source figures and how each total was calculated | Information gathering: S/N |
| Both are asked for a view on the same proposal | Clarify a view by discussing the evidence with others | Clarify a view by reflecting privately on the same evidence | Direction of attention: E/I. Either person can use both approaches. |

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional team, either person could contact colleagues or check an equipment report when a problem comes up. The role, the information available and whoever is on duty help explain what happens.

ENFJ and ISTP differ on Extraversion and Introversion, Intuition and Sensing, Feeling and Thinking, and Judging and Perceiving. Each pair addresses a different question:

- E/I: in a meeting, does the clue more often come from the exchange, or from one's own sorting?
- S/N: from the same material, does one more often read fact and precedent, or trend and other possibilities?
- T/F: for the same decision, does one more often ask whether the standard is consistent, or who will be affected?
- J/P: for the same matter, does one more often fix the checkpoints, or leave room?

The four-letter codes and the function stacks describe different things. Here, all four letters differ even though the same four function labels appear in the stacks.

### ENFJ and ISTP: the weekly call that will not settle — same people, two slots

In this fictional team, five people work in New York, one in Berlin and one in Singapore. The team has two proposed meeting windows. These local times use a November example and can shift with daylight saving time:

- Window A: 8 a.m. New York, 2 p.m. Berlin, 9 p.m. Singapore.
- Window B: 10 a.m. Singapore, 3 a.m. Berlin, 9 p.m. the previous evening in New York.

Neither option fits everyone’s usual workday. Option A gives the Singapore colleague an evening meeting. Option B falls overnight in Berlin and the previous evening in New York. The group can weigh those costs against the need to meet live.

Given the same schedule, either organizer can consider who would be excluded and how often the same people would be asked to join outside their usual hours. Either can also apply the same criteria to each option and check which agenda items need a live discussion. Those questions illustrate T/F.

Either organizer could propose a rotating time or move more of the work to written updates. The choice depends on attendance needs, the information available and what the meeting needs to settle.

Keep the counterexamples. An ENFJ who has sat through weeks of calls with no conclusion will also say to cancel the call; an ISTP wanting a new joiner to catch the first one will also agree to move to an inconvenient hour. Both only show that either can take the other's approach; neither assigns a type.

To tell them apart, do not watch the order. A more usable question: what information did you use this time, and by what standard did you weigh it? If the role changed — you are convening rather than invited, or the deadline compresses from a week to a day — would you choose the other option? The answer is more stable in what changes when conditions change than in who moved first.

The one line before the meeting can stay, but it reviews the plan, not the type: each writes one sentence on the one thing this meeting has to settle, and afterwards check whether it was settled and where the unsettled part went. If neither can write it, the meeting should be merged or cancelled; if five things get listed, it should be split. The exercise works for both types.

Sitting first does not mean someone is necessarily faster at that kind of work; sitting last does not mean they cannot do it. The third position needs the same statement. compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: what follows concerns scheduling and communication, not equipment operation, medical judgement or emergency response, which follow team procedure and professional guidance. The division of work need not be drawn by type either: who owns coverage and who owns the case for synchrony follows role, experience, available time and rotation, and one person can hold both.

### ENFJ and ISTP: the cross-timezone call — rotate the slot, or go asynchronous

(Fictional scene) Seven people in three places, and only windows A and B available. One approach rotates: A in odd months, B in even months, the sync compressed to thirty minutes, the agenda sent two days ahead, everything else written down. The benefit is that the inconvenience alternates between two places and nobody is pinned to 9 p.m. or 3 a.m. for good; the cost is a moving hour, a calendar someone always misreads, and a rotation table that needs maintaining.

A second option is to share reports a day ahead and use a short call only for decisions that need live discussion. If that call always uses option A, the after-hours burden still falls on the Singapore colleague. Written, recorded or live input can give colleagues more than one way to contribute.

A workable combination fixes the two decisions separately: sync frequency fixed at the first Tuesday of each month, the hour rotating between A and B; material sent two days ahead; the meeting handling only what cannot be written clearly. That way "how often" is stable and "what time" rotates, and neither has to be renegotiated each time.

The review looks at three things rather than at whether anyone raised something new: which items closed without a conclusion, whether anyone responded in the asynchronous thread, and where the burden fell (who has been online at an inconvenient hour for months, who has not spoken for months). If the burden concentrates in one place for long, reorder the rotation or move more content to async; if the async thread goes unanswered for long, text does not work for this group and the sync time has to come back.

### ENFJ and ISTP: a video call with grandmother — one gathering, or two

(Fictional scene) Three members of the family are in three cities and grandmother is at home. One approach gathers everyone on one evening, even if it means waiting until ten, so it is all said at once; the other splits it into two ten-minute calls, whoever is free calls, and grandmother does not sit watching the screen waiting for everyone to arrive.

Each has a cost: gathering once makes the older person's routine give way to the younger ones' schedules, and one person's late meeting cancels the whole thing; splitting means two calls for her, and the liveliness is diluted.

This is not about who is more dutiful. The one gathering often worries that "together" itself will not be conveyed and she will feel fobbed off; the one splitting often worries that she stays up to ten only to see a few faces, and that seeing is more important than seeing at the same time. Both worries can hold at once, and the same person may switch between months: having gathered last time, they are willing to split this time; with her health poor lately, someone who argued for splitting may want to gather.

The counterexamples need stating: an ENFJ will also say it is too late today and call separately tomorrow; an ISTP will also fix the time two weeks ahead for her birthday. The evidence is not who gave way this time, and not the proportion across a few cases in the same direction, but which kind of reason recurs across comparable situations.

Ask the grandmother what time and format she prefers. If she wants one shared call, the family can check whether an earlier time works. If she prefers shorter calls, they can agree when to call. Participation and feedback can show whether the arrangement works.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread uses warmth as the dividing line. An ENFJ may greet strangers first; an ISTP may say three sentences all evening, all of them at the critical moment. In the other direction, an ENFJ has days of not wanting to talk, and an ISTP can have a table laughing. Social performance depends on setting, role and the day's state, and cannot replace a judgement of preference.

The second writes the difference as a ranking of ability, or as a job allocation. Being able to organise people does not mean being more mature, and being able to take a problem apart does not mean being more professional; Ti does not mean the one who fixes equipment, and Fe does not mean the one who handles interpersonal coordination. Turn a preference into a score or a post table and every later observation distorts.

The third comes from "all four letters differ, so there is nothing in common". This pair is the opposite: no letter shared, yet all four function names identical. Reading only the letters suggests no common language; reading only the names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth uses the order of one action as a test. "He asked people first, so he leans F" almost never holds from a single event: asking people first may be because he is convening, and calculating the window first may be because something else is due tomorrow.

Not a division by type. Coverage and the case for synchrony both have to be owned by someone, and who does which follows role, experience, available time and rotation, not an assessment result.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: In a fictional team, either person could contact colleagues or check an equipment report when a problem comes up. The role, the information available and whoever is on duty help explain what happens.
ENFJ and ISTP differ on Extraversion and Introversion, Intuition and Sensing, Feeling and Thinking, and Judging and Perceiving. Each pair addresses a different question:

- E/I: in a meeting, does the clue more often come from the exchange, or from one's own sorting?
- S/N: from the same material, does one more often read fact and precedent, or trend and other possibilities?
- T/F: for the same decision, does one more often ask whether the standard is consistent, or who will be affected?
- J/P: for the same matter, does one more often fix the checkpoints, or leave room?
The four-letter codes and the function stacks describe different things. Here, all four letters differ even though the same four function labels appear in the stacks.
### ENFJ and ISTP: the weekly call that will not settle — same people, two slots

In this fictional team, five people work in New York, one in Berlin and one in Singapore. The team has two proposed meeting windows. These local times use a November example and can shift with daylight saving time:

- Window A: 8 a.m. New York, 2 p.m. Berlin, 9 p.m. Singapore.
- Window B: 10 a.m. Singapore, 3 a.m. Berlin, 9 p.m. the previous evening in New York.

Neither option fits everyone’s usual workday. Option A gives the Singapore colleague an evening meeting. Option B falls overnight in Berlin and the previous evening in New York. The group can weigh those costs against the need to meet live.

Given the same schedule, either organizer can consider who would be excluded and how often the same people would be asked to join outside their usual hours. Either can also apply the same criteria to each option and check which agenda items need a live discussion. Those questions illustrate T/F.
Either organizer could propose a rotating time or move more of the work to written updates. The choice depends on attendance needs, the information available and what the meeting needs to settle.

Keep the counterexamples. An ENFJ who has sat through weeks of calls with no conclusion will also say to cancel the call; an ISTP wanting a new joiner to catch the first one will also agree to move to an inconvenient hour. Both only show that either can take the other's approach; neither assigns a type.

To tell them apart, do not watch the order. A more usable question: what information did you use this time, and by what standard did you weigh it? If the role changed — you are convening rather than invited, or the deadline compresses from a week to a day — would you choose the other option? The answer is more stable in what changes when conditions change than in who moved first.

The one line before the meeting can stay, but it reviews the plan, not the type: each writes one sentence on the one thing this meeting has to settle, and afterwards check whether it was settled and where the unsettled part went. If neither can write it, the meeting should be merged or cancelled; if five things get listed, it should be split. The exercise works for both types.
### ENFJ and ISTP: why the four names match while the order reverses

Line the two stacks up: Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. ENFJ's first, Fe, lands fourth in ISTP; ENFJ's fourth, Ti, is first in ISTP; Ni and Se swap in between. All four names appear on both sides, in exactly reversed order.

The nature of this writing needs stating. In the common four-function notation used here, the four positions correspond to dominant, auxiliary, third and inferior; it describes emphasis inside the model, not a scale of ability and not a table of difficulty. Sitting first does not mean someone is necessarily faster at that kind of work; sitting last does not mean they cannot do it. Reading the dominant as a person's ceiling and the inferior as their weakness turns the model into a verdict on ability, which this page does not do.

The third position needs the same statement. ENFJ's Se and ISTP's Ni sit third, and whether those processes should be marked introverted or extraverted is handled differently across sources: some give only the name, some give an attitude. The steadier formulation is that, in the writing used here, both types carry the same four attitude-marked functions in reversed order, while the attitude of the third process is not labelled the same way everywhere. Where versions disagree, see which notation is being cited, then read the divergence through the first two positions. Full descriptions sit at the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

body: This table covers six observation points inside the meeting, with the conditions fixed: the same people, the same matter, the same two available windows, A and B. If one of them is convening and the other merely invited, or one has been on this team for three years, role and experience will swamp both columns. The rows describe evidence that may get more attention, not who speaks earlier or executes better; either type may take either approach in the same row.

| Observation point in the meeting | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ISTP: evidence likely to be attended to first | Which axis this row lands on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to hold this call, and for how long | Weigh how each workable meeting option affects those who would otherwise be left out | Apply the same criteria for synchronous discussion to all workable options | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both plan the same meeting while the same papers are pending | Agree on a provisional agenda and a time to revisit it | Keep two workable agenda options open until the papers arrive | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both review the same mismatch in the report | Look for a pattern across comparable discrepancies and list possible shared causes | Check the source figures and how each total was calculated | Information gathering: S/N |
| Both are asked for a view on the same proposal | Clarify a view by discussing the evidence with others | Clarify a view by reflecting privately on the same evidence | Direction of attention: E/I. Either person can use both approaches. |
| Someone has not spoken in the call for weeks | Weigh what the same participation record means for the person and the people they work with | Apply the same criterion for whose input is needed to each decision in the record | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Looking back on this arrangement in three months | Under which conditions this arrangement fails, and whether another group could copy it | Whether the call got shorter, how many decisions landed, and which month went wrong | What counts as material, leaning S/N |

None of these rows is a scale of ability, and none can be used to classify. The same person may land on any row in a different month: an ISTP who has coordinated remotely for three years will maintain the rotation table unprompted, and an ENFJ just moved from the front line into a project group may calculate the windows first. Role, duty, experience and deadline all rewrite these rows.

body: Boundary of use: what follows concerns scheduling and communication, not equipment operation, medical judgement or emergency response, which follow team procedure and professional guidance. The division of work need not be drawn by type either: who owns coverage and who owns the case for synchrony follows role, experience, available time and rotation, and one person can hold both.
### ENFJ and ISTP: the cross-timezone call — rotate the slot, or go asynchronous

(Fictional scene) Seven people in three places, and only windows A and B available. One approach rotates: A in odd months, B in even months, the sync compressed to thirty minutes, the agenda sent two days ahead, everything else written down. The benefit is that the inconvenience alternates between two places and nobody is pinned to 9 p.m. or 3 a.m. for good; the cost is a moving hour, a calendar someone always misreads, and a rotation table that needs maintaining.

A second option is to share reports a day ahead and use a short call only for decisions that need live discussion. If that call always uses option A, the after-hours burden still falls on the Singapore colleague. Written, recorded or live input can give colleagues more than one way to contribute.

A workable combination fixes the two decisions separately: sync frequency fixed at the first Tuesday of each month, the hour rotating between A and B; material sent two days ahead; the meeting handling only what cannot be written clearly. That way "how often" is stable and "what time" rotates, and neither has to be renegotiated each time.

The review looks at three things rather than at whether anyone raised something new: which items closed without a conclusion, whether anyone responded in the asynchronous thread, and where the burden fell (who has been online at an inconvenient hour for months, who has not spoken for months). If the burden concentrates in one place for long, reorder the rotation or move more content to async; if the async thread goes unanswered for long, text does not work for this group and the sync time has to come back.
### ENFJ and ISTP: a video call with grandmother — one gathering, or two

(Fictional scene) Three members of the family are in three cities and grandmother is at home. One approach gathers everyone on one evening, even if it means waiting until ten, so it is all said at once; the other splits it into two ten-minute calls, whoever is free calls, and grandmother does not sit watching the screen waiting for everyone to arrive.

Each has a cost: gathering once makes the older person's routine give way to the younger ones' schedules, and one person's late meeting cancels the whole thing; splitting means two calls for her, and the liveliness is diluted.

This is not about who is more dutiful. The one gathering often worries that "together" itself will not be conveyed and she will feel fobbed off; the one splitting often worries that she stays up to ten only to see a few faces, and that seeing is more important than seeing at the same time. Both worries can hold at once, and the same person may switch between months: having gathered last time, they are willing to split this time; with her health poor lately, someone who argued for splitting may want to gather.

The counterexamples need stating: an ENFJ will also say it is too late today and call separately tomorrow; an ISTP will also fix the time two weeks ahead for her birthday. The evidence is not who gave way this time, and not the proportion across a few cases in the same direction, but which kind of reason recurs across comparable situations.

Ask the grandmother what time and format she prefers. If she wants one shared call, the family can check whether an earlier time works. If she prefers shorter calls, they can agree when to call. Participation and feedback can show whether the arrangement works.

body: The first misread uses warmth as the dividing line. An ENFJ may greet strangers first; an ISTP may say three sentences all evening, all of them at the critical moment. In the other direction, an ENFJ has days of not wanting to talk, and an ISTP can have a table laughing. Social performance depends on setting, role and the day's state, and cannot replace a judgement of preference.

The second writes the difference as a ranking of ability, or as a job allocation. Being able to organise people does not mean being more mature, and being able to take a problem apart does not mean being more professional; Ti does not mean the one who fixes equipment, and Fe does not mean the one who handles interpersonal coordination. Turn a preference into a score or a post table and every later observation distorts.

The third comes from "all four letters differ, so there is nothing in common". This pair is the opposite: no letter shared, yet all four function names identical. Reading only the letters suggests no common language; reading only the names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth uses the order of one action as a test. "He asked people first, so he leans F" almost never holds from a single event: asking people first may be because he is convening, and calculating the window first may be because something else is due tomorrow.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring definition first, then recall where you stood during that period: had you just taken on cross-department coordination, had you just been moved to a delivery-only project. Circumstances push answers toward one side, but that push is hard to direct at a particular type; note it as background and do not use it to explain the result.

The practice needs no set number of cases. Take a few recent occasions that genuinely required fixing a time and write three lines for each: what information was used, by what standard it was weighed (people's convenience, the necessity of the matter, or both), and whether a change of role or deadline would have led to the other choice. After a while, if "who is left out" and "does this have to be synchronous" keep recurring, that is worth discussing as your habit of gathering and judging; it is reflective material, not a typing rule.

If the report gives per-axis results, check the version and scoring notes first, then go axis by axis: which axes changed between sittings, and which stay close to a boundary. ENFJ and ISTP differ on all four, so one axis near a boundary only means that label is sensitive to changes in answering; it does not mean both types hold at once. The steadier move is to take that one axis and review the evidence across several comparable situations, rather than jumping to the other type wholesale.

body: **Framework sources** Preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Four-position convention on this page** The arrangement of the four positions here, in particular the attitude of the third process, follows a common writing adopted as an editorial convention; other sources handle it differently, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading.

**Editorial fiction note** The cross-timezone call and the family video call are editorial fiction, corresponding to no real team, company or household, written to illustrate scheduling decisions, and constituting no advice beyond scheduling and communication.

**Scope limits** The four axes and the function positions describe emphasis between preferences; they do not predict behaviour order, areas of strength, whether collaboration will go smoothly, or attraction. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships. If the role changed — you are convening rather than invited, or the deadline compresses from a week to a day — would you choose the other option? The answer is more stable in what changes when conditions change than in who moved first.

The one line before the meeting can stay, but it reviews the plan, not the type: each writes one sentence on the one thing this meeting has to settle, and afterwards check whether it was settled and where the unsettled part went. If neither can write it, the meeting should be merged or cancelled; if five things get listed, it should be split. The exercise works for both types.

### ENFJ and ISTP: why the four names match while the order reverses

Line the two stacks up: Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. ENFJ's first, Fe, lands fourth in ISTP; ENFJ's fourth, Ti, is first in ISTP; Ni and Se swap in between. All four names appear on both sides, in exactly reversed order.

The nature of this writing needs stating. In the common four-function notation used here, the four positions correspond to dominant, auxiliary, third and inferior; it describes emphasis inside the model, not a scale of ability and not a table of difficulty. Sitting first does not mean someone is necessarily faster at that kind of work; sitting last does not mean they cannot do it. Reading the dominant as a person's ceiling and the inferior as their weakness turns the model into a verdict on ability, which this page does not do.

The third position needs the same statement. ENFJ's Se and ISTP's Ni sit third, and whether those processes should be marked introverted or extraverted is handled differently across sources: some give only the name, some give an attitude. The steadier formulation is that, in the writing used here, both types carry the same four attitude-marked functions in reversed order, while the attitude of the third process is not labelled the same way everywhere. Where versions disagree, see which notation is being cited, then read the divergence through the first two positions. Full descriptions sit at the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

sections.body_md:
This table covers six observation points inside the meeting, with the conditions fixed: the same people, the same matter, the same two available windows, A and B. If one of them is convening and the other merely invited, or one has been on this team for three years, role and experience will swamp both columns. The rows describe evidence that may get more attention, not who speaks earlier or executes better; either type may take either approach in the same row.

| Observation point in the meeting | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ISTP: evidence likely to be attended to first | Which axis this row lands on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to hold this call, and for how long | Weigh how each workable meeting option affects those who would otherwise be left out | Apply the same criteria for synchronous discussion to all workable options | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both plan the same meeting while the same papers are pending | Agree on a provisional agenda and a time to revisit it | Keep two workable agenda options open until the papers arrive | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both review the same mismatch in the report | Look for a pattern across comparable discrepancies and list possible shared causes | Check the source figures and how each total was calculated | Information gathering: S/N |
| Both are asked for a view on the same proposal | Clarify a view by discussing the evidence with others | Clarify a view by reflecting privately on the same evidence | Direction of attention: E/I. Either person can use both approaches. |
| Someone has not spoken in the call for weeks | Weigh what the same participation record means for the person and the people they work with | Apply the same criterion for whose input is needed to each decision in the record | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Looking back on this arrangement in three months | Under which conditions this arrangement fails, and whether another group could copy it | Whether the call got shorter, how many decisions landed, and which month went wrong | What counts as material, leaning S/N |

None of these rows is a scale of ability, and none can be used to classify. The same person may land on any row in a different month: an ISTP who has coordinated remotely for three years will maintain the rotation table unprompted, and an ENFJ just moved from the front line into a project group may calculate the windows first. Role, duty, experience and deadline all rewrite these rows.

sections.body_md:
Boundary of use: what follows concerns scheduling and communication, not equipment operation, medical judgement or emergency response, which follow team procedure and professional guidance. The division of work need not be drawn by type either: who owns coverage and who owns the case for synchrony follows role, experience, available time and rotation, and one person can hold both.

### ENFJ and ISTP: the cross-timezone call — rotate the slot, or go asynchronous

(Fictional scene) Seven people in three places, and only windows A and B available. One approach rotates: A in odd months, B in even months, the sync compressed to thirty minutes, the agenda sent two days ahead, everything else written down. The benefit is that the inconvenience alternates between two places and nobody is pinned to 9 p.m. or 3 a.m. for good; the cost is a moving hour, a calendar someone always misreads, and a rotation table that needs maintaining.

A second option is to share reports a day ahead and use a short call only for decisions that need live discussion. If that call always uses option A, the after-hours burden still falls on the Singapore colleague. Written, recorded or live input can give colleagues more than one way to contribute.

A workable combination fixes the two decisions separately: sync frequency fixed at the first Tuesday of each month, the hour rotating between A and B; material sent two days ahead; the meeting handling only what cannot be written clearly. That way "how often" is stable and "what time" rotates, and neither has to be renegotiated each time.

The review looks at three things rather than at whether anyone raised something new: which items closed without a conclusion, whether anyone responded in the asynchronous thread, and where the burden fell (who has been online at an inconvenient hour for months, who has not spoken for months). If the burden concentrates in one place for long, reorder the rotation or move more content to async; if the async thread goes unanswered for long, text does not work for this group and the sync time has to come back.

### ENFJ and ISTP: a video call with grandmother — one gathering, or two

(Fictional scene) Three members of the family are in three cities and grandmother is at home. One approach gathers everyone on one evening, even if it means waiting until ten, so it is all said at once; the other splits it into two ten-minute calls, whoever is free calls, and grandmother does not sit watching the screen waiting for everyone to arrive.

Each has a cost: gathering once makes the older person's routine give way to the younger ones' schedules, and one person's late meeting cancels the whole thing; splitting means two calls for her, and the liveliness is diluted.

This is not about who is more dutiful. The one gathering often worries that "together" itself will not be conveyed and she will feel fobbed off; the one splitting often worries that she stays up to ten only to see a few faces, and that seeing is more important than seeing at the same time. Both worries can hold at once, and the same person may switch between months: having gathered last time, they are willing to split this time; with her health poor lately, someone who argued for splitting may want to gather.

The counterexamples need stating: an ENFJ will also say it is too late today and call separately tomorrow; an ISTP will also fix the time two weeks ahead for her birthday. The evidence is not who gave way this time, and not the proportion across a few cases in the same direction, but which kind of reason recurs across comparable situations.

Ask the grandmother what time and format she prefers. If she wants one shared call, the family can check whether an earlier time works. If she prefers shorter calls, they can agree when to call. Participation and feedback can show whether the arrangement works.

sections.body_md:
The first misread uses warmth as the dividing line. An ENFJ may greet strangers first; an ISTP may say three sentences all evening, all of them at the critical moment. In the other direction, an ENFJ has days of not wanting to talk, and an ISTP can have a table laughing. Social performance depends on setting, role and the day's state, and cannot replace a judgement of preference.

The second writes the difference as a ranking of ability, or as a job allocation. Being able to organise people does not mean being more mature, and being able to take a problem apart does not mean being more professional; Ti does not mean the one who fixes equipment, and Fe does not mean the one who handles interpersonal coordination. Turn a preference into a score or a post table and every later observation distorts.

The third comes from "all four letters differ, so there is nothing in common". This pair is the opposite: no letter shared, yet all four function names identical. Reading only the letters suggests no common language; reading only the names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth uses the order of one action as a test. "He asked people first, so he leans F" almost never holds from a single event: asking people first may be because he is convening, and calculating the window first may be because something else is due tomorrow.
sections.title: ENFJ and ISTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring definition first, then recall where you stood during that period: had you just taken on cross-department coordination, had you just been moved to a delivery-only project. Circumstances push answers toward one side, but that push is hard to direct at a particular type; note it as background and do not use it to explain the result.

The practice needs no set number of cases. Take a few recent occasions that genuinely required fixing a time and write three lines for each: what information was used, by what standard it was weighed (people's convenience, the necessity of the matter, or both), and whether a change of role or deadline would have led to the other choice. After a while, if "who is left out" and "does this have to be synchronous" keep recurring, that is worth discussing as your habit of gathering and judging; it is reflective material, not a typing rule.

If the report gives per-axis results, check the version and scoring notes first, then go axis by axis: which axes changed between sittings, and which stay close to a boundary. ENFJ and ISTP differ on all four, so one axis near a boundary only means that label is sensitive to changes in answering; it does not mean both types hold at once. The steadier move is to take that one axis and review the evidence across several comparable situations, rather than jumping to the other type wholesale.

items.answer:
No — that describes the outcome of a division of work, not its basis. Whether someone manages people or things follows the post, the duty and who is present far more than type; either type can be assigned to coordinate, and either can be assigned to trace a fault.

For the fictional call, compare how each option affects participants and whether each option meets the same criteria for live discussion. Either consideration can come from either person. Neither Fe nor Ti indicates who should coordinate the meeting or handle an equipment problem.
items.question: Is the difference simply one manages people and the other manages things?

items.answer:
Because the positions differ. In the writing used here, Fe is first in ENFJ and fourth in ISTP, and Ti the reverse.

Position describes the order of emphasis inside the model (dominant, auxiliary, third, inferior), not a table of difficulty: a process sitting later does not mean it cannot be used, only that in this writing it sits later. Sources label the third process differently; that disagreement does not affect the first two positions and does not change the fact that the four names match. Full descriptions sit on the base pages.
items.question: The four function names are identical — why are these two different types?

items.answer:
As normal: either type can take the other's approach, and a single action is not evidence of belonging.

The usable distinction is not who is more tired but the reason: across comparable situations, does he more often cite who will be left out and who is holding on, or whether this has to be synchronous and whether text can replace it. If the choice changes when the role or deadline changes, the condition is doing the work, not the type.
items.question: An ISTP also looks after other people's time, an ENFJ also wants to cancel the call — how does that count?

items.answer:
Not a division by type. Coverage and the case for synchrony both have to be owned by someone, and who does which follows role, experience, available time and rotation, not an assessment result.

In practice, name one owner for coverage (who is left out, who has been online at bad hours for weeks, whether the rotation is actually running) and one for necessity (whether this sync is needed, whether material can replace it, whether the technical question can be settled in the call), and agree to swap or review monthly. One person taking both is fine too; coverage alone multiplies meetings, and necessity alone lets part of the group quietly drop out.
items.question: In cross-timezone collaboration, which end should each own?

items.answer:
Usually an unstated division of work rather than the type difference.

Agree who chooses the time and format, whose input is necessary and who will make the decision if the group disagrees. A short written note can keep two people from solving different problems in parallel.
items.question: What most often drags when paired with an ENFJ or an ISTP?

items.answer:
The assessment's name, version, language and scoring definition, rather than finding an action like "how you arrange a gathering when nobody asked" to settle it.

If the item bank gives per-axis scores, go axis by axis: which changed between sittings, and which sit near a boundary. ENFJ and ISTP differ on all four, so one axis near a boundary only means that axis is sensitive, not that both types hold. Without per-axis scores or scoring notes, do not infer a near-boundary result and do not prescribe a retest interval — what can be done is to note the circumstances of each sitting and, after a while, review the evidence across several comparable situations.

**Four-position convention on this page** The arrangement of the four positions here, in particular the attitude of the third process, follows a common writing adopted as an editorial convention; other sources handle it differently, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading.

**Editorial fiction note** The cross-timezone call and the family video call are editorial fiction, corresponding to no real team, company or household, written to illustrate scheduling decisions, and constituting no advice beyond scheduling and communication.

**Scope limits** The four axes and the function positions describe emphasis between preferences; they do not predict behaviour order, areas of strength, whether collaboration will go smoothly, or attraction. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships.
